cards.front: What three demands must a genetic material meet?
cards.back: It must store a great deal of information that differs among individuals and species; be copied faithfully before cell division; and act by directing what the cell makes.
cards.quote: A genetic material must store a great deal of information that differs among individuals and species.

cards.front: Why did protein, not DNA, look like the better genetic material candidate before the transformation and phage experiments?
cards.back: Protein has about 20 amino-acid building blocks, while DNA has four bases and was thought to repeat simply.
cards.quote: Protein looked the better candidate: it has about 20 amino-acid building blocks, while DNA has four bases and was thought to repeat simply.

cards.front: In pneumococcus, smooth (S) strains have a {{c1::capsule}} and can kill a mouse; rough (R) variants lack it and are generally harmless.
cards.quote: Smooth (S) strains have a capsule and can kill a mouse; rough (R) variants lack it and are generally harmless.
cards.section: From a heritable change to an assay

cards.front: In Griffith's 1928 design, mice received a small dose of living rough bacteria derived from type II together with heat-killed type III smooth bacteria. What was recovered from the mice that died, and what does it show?
cards.back: Living, encapsulated type III bacteria that bred true. Something from the dead type III cells heritably changed the living rough cells.
cards.why: A control series showed the heated culture was sterile.
cards.quote: Some mice died, and from them Griffith recovered living, encapsulated type III bacteria that bred true.
cards.section: From a heritable change to an assay

cards.front: Griffith's experiment showed that something in dead S cells changed living R cells. What did it leave unidentified, and what did Griffith suggest?
cards.back: The chemical identity of the transforming principle was left open. Griffith suggested a specific protein structure in the dead cells.
cards.quote: Griffith suggested that a specific protein structure in the dead cells let the living ones make the capsule.
cards.section: From a heritable change to an assay

cards.front: Griffith left an assay, a scored experimental readout: {{c1::transformation}} to the donor's type, kept by descendants.
cards.quote: He left an assay, a scored experimental readout: transformation to the donor's type, kept by descendants.
cards.section: From a heritable change to an assay

cards.front: In the 1944 purification of the active fraction from type III cells, which two measurements matched nucleic acid?
cards.back: The nitrogen-to-phosphorus ratio and the ultraviolet absorption.
cards.quote: In their 1944 paper, the nitrogen-to-phosphorus ratio and ultraviolet absorption matched nucleic acid.
cards.section: From a heritable change to an assay

cards.front: In a transformation assay, a protease preparation is added and activity is unchanged. Why must the preparation first be shown to digest a known protein before this means anything?
cards.back: Unchanged activity is informative only if the enzyme was active. A failed protease could leave a protein agent untouched. Digestion of its known target makes "activity remained" evidence against protein being required.
cards.quote: An unchanged transformation assay is informative only if the enzyme was active.
cards.section: From a heritable change to an assay

cards.front: A purified transforming fraction keeps full activity after trypsin plus chymotrypsin and after ribonuclease, but loses all activity after DNase. What do these results show about this bacterial fraction?
cards.back: Its activity requires intact DNA. It survives treatments that digest most protein and RNA.
cards.quote: Claim: activity requires intact DNA and survives treatments that digest most protein and RNA.
cards.section: Design problem: make the claim no larger than the data

cards.front: Avery, MacLeod and McCarty concluded the principle was "principally, if not solely" DNA. What objection did that hedge leave open?
cards.back: A protein below the detection limit might be the real agent, with DNA as its carrier.
cards.quote: The hedge left one objection open: a protein below the detection limit might be the real agent, with DNA as its carrier.
cards.section: From a heritable change to an assay

cards.front: A critic proposes that a protein below 0.1% is the real transforming agent. Why can the enzyme data alone not rule this out, and what purification test would make the critic's view harder to defend?
cards.back: A detection limit cannot prove a trace protein is absent, and it might resist the proteases used. Follow activity during purification: if activity per microgram of DNA stays constant while protein falls tenfold or more, a protein contaminant is harder to defend.
cards.quote: Limit: a detection limit cannot prove that a trace protein is absent, and that protein might resist the proteases used.
cards.section: Design problem: make the claim no larger than the data

cards.front: DNA preparations were later shown to transfer other traits, such as drug resistance, and not only capsule type. Why does this strain a trace-protein explanation of transformation?
cards.back: A protein account would need a different trait-specific contaminant for each preparation.
cards.quote: A protein account would then need a different trait-specific contaminant for each preparation.
cards.section: Design problem: make the claim no larger than the data

cards.front: {{c1::Cysteine and methionine}} put sulfur in protein, while DNA has none.
cards.quote: Cysteine and methionine put sulfur in protein, while DNA has none.
cards.section: An independent tracer test

cards.front: Why does phosphorus-32 label mostly DNA in the Hershey and Chase design?
cards.back: DNA's backbone is rich in phosphorus, while protein has little.
cards.quote: DNA's backbone is rich in phosphorus, while protein has little.
cards.section: An independent tracer test

cards.front: Phage T2 labelled with sulfur-35 or phosphorus-32 infects E. coli, then the mixture is blended and centrifuged. About 75% of the sulfur-35 but only about 15% of the phosphorus-32 is in the fluid. Progeny carry less than 1% of parental sulfur and 30% or more of parental phosphorus. What do the data support?
cards.back: Most DNA entered the cells and much reached progeny; most coat stayed out. Heredity followed the DNA label.
cards.quote: Progeny carried less than 1% of parental sulfur and 30% or more of parental phosphorus.
cards.section: An independent tracer test

cards.front: Why do the Hershey and Chase data not show that no protein entered the cells?
cards.back: About a quarter of the sulfur stayed with the cells, and entry of sulfur-free material other than DNA was left undetermined.
cards.quote: a quarter of the sulfur stayed with the cells, so the result supports
cards.section: An independent tracer test

cards.front: Why does the phage tracer result strengthen the case from the pneumococcal enzyme experiments, rather than merely repeating it?
cards.back: It tests an independent system with a different method. Together the two made DNA the strongest candidate in these systems, though neither experiment is universal by itself.
cards.quote: Together, the 1944 and phage results made DNA the strongest candidate in these systems without making either experiment universal by itself.
cards.section: Design problem: make the claim no larger than the data

cards.front: Chargaff measured base composition in DNA from many sources. How did composition vary among species, and what did that argue against?
cards.back: Composition varied among species, which argued against a simple repeating structure.
cards.quote: Composition varied among species, arguing against a simple repeat.
cards.section: The double helix: constraints before a model

cards.front: In Chargaff's measurements, within each DNA sample {{c1::A was close to T and G close to C}}.
cards.quote: Within each sample, A was close to T and G close to C.
cards.section: The double helix: constraints before a model

cards.front: Pairing requires A = T and G = C across a duplex as a whole. What does Chargaff's second rule add, and does pairing require it?
cards.back: Each strand of most double-stranded genomes also comes close to A = T and G = C. Pairing does not require this.
cards.quote: Each strand of most double-stranded genomes also comes close to A = T and G = C. This is Chargaff's second rule; pairing does not require it.
cards.section: Chargaff's second rule

cards.front: What could X-ray fibre diffraction of DNA constrain, and what could it not reveal?
cards.back: It constrained repeated geometry but could not reveal base order.
cards.quote: Diffraction could constrain repeated geometry, but not reveal base order.
cards.section: The double helix: constraints before a model

cards.front: B-form DNA fibres showed a 3.4-angstrom spacing and a 34-angstrom repeat. Taking 3.4 angstrom as the rise per base pair, how many base pairs fit in one repeat, and how does that compare with the 1953 model?
cards.back: 34 ÷ 3.4 = 10 base pairs per repeat, which matches the 1953 model's 10 base pairs per turn.
cards.quote: The 1953 model assumed 10 base pairs per turn.
cards.section: The double helix: constraints before a model

cards.front: In the Watson and Crick double helix, which parts face outward and inward, and which bases pair?
cards.back: Phosphates face outward. Bases face inward and pair by hydrogen bonds: adenine with thymine, guanine with cytosine.
cards.quote: Phosphates face outward. Bases face inward and pair by hydrogen bonds: adenine with thymine, guanine with cytosine.
cards.section: The double helix: constraints before a model

cards.front: The two DNA chains run in opposite directions: they are {{c1::antiparallel}}.
cards.quote: The chains run in opposite directions, like the film's rails: they are antiparallel.
cards.section: The double helix: constraints before a model

cards.front: How many hydrogen bonds are in a G-C pair and an A-T pair, and what else contributes greatly to helix stability?
cards.back: Three in G-C, two in A-T. Stacking between flat bases contributes greatly to helix stability.
cards.quote: Modern structures show three hydrogen bonds in a G-C pair and two in an A-T pair, but stacking between flat bases contributes greatly to helix stability
cards.section: The double helix: constraints before a model

cards.front: Two B-form DNA segments have the same number of base pairs, but one has more G-C pairs. Is one segment longer?
cards.back: No. Length is base pairs times the rise per base pair, and hydrogen-bond counts do not enter. Equal base-pair counts give equal calculated lengths.
cards.quote: Length is base pairs times the rise per base pair.
cards.section: The double helix: constraints before a model

cards.front: A double-stranded DNA sample is 22% A. What percentages are T, G and C?
cards.back: T = 22%, G = 28%, C = 28%. A = T, leaving 56% for G plus C, and G = C.
cards.quote: A = T, G = C, and A + T + G + C = 100% in double-stranded DNA.
cards.section: Work from the pairing rules

cards.front: A viral genome has A 25%, T 33%, G 24% and C 18%. What do the ratios say about strandedness?
cards.back: It is single-stranded DNA. The bases total 100%, but A does not equal T and G does not equal C, so under perfect pairing they are not paired across two strands.
cards.quote: The bases total 100%, but A does not equal T and G does not equal C.
cards.section: Work from the pairing rules

cards.front: A linear B-form duplex is 8,400 bp, with a rise of 0.34 nm per base pair and about 10.5 bp per turn. What are its length and number of turns?
cards.back: Length = 8,400 × 0.34 nm = 2,856 nm, about 2.9 micrometres. Turns = 8,400 ÷ 10.5 = 800.
cards.quote: length = 3,000 × 0.34 nm = 1,020 nm, about 1.0 micrometre turns = 3,000 ÷ 10.5 = 285.7, about 286
cards.section: Work from the pairing rules

cards.front: A student doubles the rise per base pair when calculating the length of a duplex, because it has two strands. Why is this wrong?
cards.back: The rise is per base pair, and one base pair already spans both strands.
cards.quote: Rise is per base pair, so do not double it for two strands.
cards.section: Work from the pairing rules

cards.front: For helix dimensions, a {{c1::base pair}} (bp) is one paired position across the two strands.
cards.quote: For helix dimensions, a base pair, abbreviated bp, is one paired position across the two strands.
cards.section: Work from the pairing rules

cards.front: One strand of a DNA segment reads 5'-ATGCCA-3'. Write the partner strand 5' to 3'.
cards.back: 5'-TGGCAT-3'. Pairing gives TACGGT, then the order is reversed because the strands are antiparallel.
cards.quote: To write a partner 5' to 3', pair the bases and then reverse the order, because the strands are antiparallel.
cards.section: From complement to copying

cards.front: Which feature of the double helix suggested a way to copy a gene?
cards.back: Specific pairing means one strand fixes the sequence of its partner, so if the chains separate each can serve as a template for a new partner.
cards.quote: In a second Nature paper later in 1953, Watson and Crick proposed that the chains separate and each serves as a template for a new partner.
cards.section: From complement to copying

cards.front: E. coli grown for many generations on heavy nitrogen are moved to light nitrogen, and DNA is separated by density. If each new double helix keeps one parental strand and gets one new strand, what is expected after one and after two generations?
cards.back: After one: all hybrid. After two: equal hybrid and light. Each new duplex holds one parental strand and one new strand.
cards.quote: They grew E. coli on heavy nitrogen, moved it to light nitrogen and separated DNA by density: all hybrid after one generation, equal hybrid and light after two.
cards.section: From complement to copying

cards.front: Extending the heavy-to-light nitrogen density experiment, what fractions of hybrid and light DNA are expected after three generations if each new duplex keeps one parental strand?
cards.back: One quarter hybrid, three quarters light. Hybrid fraction halves each generation under the stated rule (all, one half, one quarter).
cards.quote: They grew E. coli on heavy nitrogen, moved it to light nitrogen and separated DNA by density: all hybrid after one generation, equal hybrid and light after two.
cards.section: From complement to copying

cards.front: What does complementary pairing explain about DNA copying, and what does it not supply?
cards.back: It supplies sequence information for the new strand, not the machinery of replication.
cards.quote: pairing supplies sequence information, not the machinery of replication.
